summary: Proposes an experimental set of alternative decision-making processes for IETF working groups. It targets the rare cases where a group agrees a decision must be made but cannot agree on what the decision should be. The processes are experiments, and the document does not claim to be exhaustive.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 3929 describes four experimental ways to choose among proposals when an IETF working group cannot reach agreement. The normal rough-consensus process remains the starting point, and the group is not required to use an alternative.

subtitle: Experimental tie-breaking processes for rare IETF working-group deadlocks.

tldr.problem: An IETF working group can agree that it must choose one technical proposal yet fail to reach rough consensus on which proposal to advance.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC sets conditions for considering an alternative and describes four methods: an external review team, a mixed review team, a qualified short-straw decision maker, or random assignment by IANA.
tldr.outcome: These methods are an experiment and do not replace the normal consensus process. RFC 3929 is updated by RFC 8717.

today: RFC 3929 is an Experimental RFC and is updated by RFC 8717. Its text says a method should be documented in a Best Current Practice only if the community finds it useful.

sections.title: When a Technical Choice Is Blocked
sections.content:
The RFC addresses a narrow case: a working group agrees that it must make a technical decision, but cannot agree which of two or more similarly mature proposals to advance. The document does not propose changing the IETF's usual decision process.

The methods are experimental and are intended for cases where continued discussion, specification work, and implementation experience have not resolved the choice. An alternative process should not take precedence over rough consensus.
sections.plainLanguage: The group must agree that a choice is necessary before considering a tie-breaker. The regular consensus process remains the default.

sections.title: Conditions Before Using an Alternative
sections.content:
The decision must be clearly stated, and the proposals must be available as sufficiently detailed Internet-Drafts. The working group must discuss the technical issues and make an explicit consensus call; if new technical points arise, discussion continues.

A separate working-group Last Call must ask whether to use an alternative method. Rough consensus is required to invoke one, but the working group is never required to do so. If the group agrees to use a method but cannot agree which one, the RFC specifies an external review team.
sections.plainLanguage: Before a tie-breaker, the group needs a clear decision, written proposals, and enough discussion. Members must also reach rough consensus to use an alternative process.

sections.title: Four Ways to Reach a Decision
sections.content:
The external review team has five eligible members who rank proposals in short decision statements. The mixed review team combines one representative for each proposal with six external members. Both teams use instant-runoff voting to tally their rankings.

In the qualified short-straw method, one eligible working-group participant is selected from volunteers using the procedure in RFC 3797 and names the chosen draft. In the random-assignment method, IANA selects randomly among clearly defined values when the choice has no technical distinction. Each method begins with a public announcement to the IETF community.
sections.plainLanguage: The first two methods ask review teams to rank the proposals. The other methods select one qualified decision maker or use a random choice when no technical difference matters.

sections.title: Appeals and Risks
sections.content:
A decision reached through an alternative method can be appealed under the same rules as another working-group decision. The group's consensus to use the method stands in place of consensus on the technical question.

The RFC warns that alternative processes can shift how decisions are made and may be manipulated. It presents the methods as experimental tools for possible deadlocks, not as replacements for the usual process.
sections.plainLanguage: A result can be appealed under the existing rules. The RFC warns that participants could try to manipulate a process, which is one reason the alternatives remain experimental.
